lede: Green plants capture the Sun's energy, and everything else in an ecosystem eats to get a share of it. A food web maps who eats whom; the trophic levels count the steps from the plants. Where a resource is limited, organisms that need the same thing compete for it.
can: Read a food web and place organisms at the right trophic level.
Explain what an arrow means and which way it points.
List what plants and animals compete for, and explain a species decline.

md: Every meal you have ever eaten traces back to sunlight caught by a green plant. A food web draws that as arrows, and each arrow points the way the energy travels — from the thing eaten to the thing eating it.

md: **Start at the Sun.** Green plants — the **producers** — capture light energy from the Sun and store it as glucose by photosynthesis. Everything else in the web is a **consumer** and gets its energy by eating. **Level 1** is always the producers. **Level 2** holds the **primary consumers**, the animals that eat the producers. **Level 3** holds the **secondary consumers**, which eat the primary consumers, and **Level 4** the **tertiary consumers**.

prompt: In a food web, which way does an arrow point?
options: From the organism eaten to the one eating it
From the feeder to its food
Either way, as long as the pair is right
answer: From the organism eaten to the one eating it
explain: The arrow follows the energy, so it runs from the food towards the feeder.

md: An organism can sit at two levels in different chains: the blue tit here is a secondary consumer when it eats an aphid and a tertiary consumer when it eats a ladybird. The fox here eats only primary consumers, so it is a secondary consumer (Level 3) even though it is drawn at the top; the kestrel is a tertiary consumer when it eats the blue tit.

prompt: In the food web above, which organisms are at trophic Level 1?
explain: Level 1 is the producers, so it can only hold plants. March 2026 examiners saw buzzards and foxes offered for Level 1, which is four levels out.

title: What the arrow means
md: CCEA's wording is that arrows represent **consumption** and the **transfer of substances (carbon and nitrogen) and energy** through the ecosystem. So the arrow runs **from the organism that is eaten to the organism that eats it** — the direction the energy travels. Drawing it the other way round reverses the whole web, and in Summer 2025 the mark for adding the arrows was the one that separated candidates on the food-web question.

title: GCSE Biology Revision "Competition and Interdependence"
why: Competition, adaptation and interdependence in one short lesson, with predator-prey cycles drawn out. Watch it, then answer the question underneath.

prompt: An arrow is drawn from a rabbit to a fox. What does it mean?
options: the rabbit is eaten by the fox
the rabbit and the fox compete
answer: the rabbit is eaten by the fox
explain: 'Is eaten by'. The energy stored in the rabbit passes into the fox, which is why the arrow points that way.

md: **Competition** is what happens when two organisms need the same limited resource. Plants compete for **water, light, space, minerals**. Animals compete for **water, food, territory, mates**, and have to avoid **predators**. Two species competing for the same resource is not the same as one eating the other: grey squirrels take the food and nesting sites that red squirrels need, so red numbers fall, but no grey squirrel ever eats a red one.

title: Why competition can empty a wood without a single attack
md: A wood holds only so many acorns and only so many nest holes. Every one a grey squirrel takes is one a red squirrel cannot have, so fewer reds last the winter and fewer rear young.

prompt: Which resource do animals compete for but plants never do?
explain: Food. A plant makes its own by photosynthesis, so food is never on the plant list.

title: March 2026 B1 Foundation Q6 and Higher Q1 — the squirrel question
md: Asked why red squirrel numbers had fallen, **most candidates earned at least one of the two marks**, but **some wrote that the greys ate or hunted the reds**. The relationship is **competition**: the greys are larger, eat a wider range of food and take the same nest sites, so there is less left for the reds. In the same question **quite a few named a part of a tree as the energy source instead of the Sun**, and **a few mixed up the trophic levels**.

prompt: Plants compete for water, light, space and ______.
explain: Minerals, taken from the soil through the root hair cells. The four are water, light, space and minerals — food is never on the list, because a plant makes its own.

task: Start a population of rabbits with a limited food supply and no predators, and watch the population curve level off. Then add wolves and watch it again. Write one sentence naming the resource the rabbits are competing for, and one sentence saying what the wolves change. (The genetics in this simulation belongs to B2, not B1 — here you are only watching what limits a population.)

prompt: Grey squirrels were introduced to a wood and red squirrel numbers fell. What is the best explanation?
options: the greys competed with the reds for food and nest sites
the greys hunted and ate the reds
the greys carried the reds away
answer: the greys competed with the reds for food and nest sites
explain: Competition for the same limited resources. Naming it as predation is the error March 2026 examiners reported.

md:
Name the **Sun** as the energy source and green plants as **producers**.
Give the organisms at each **trophic level**.
Say what an arrow means: **is eaten by**.
List what **plants** and **animals** compete for.
Explain a fall in red squirrels as **competition**.

Normally the opening question, eight to twelve marks hung on one habitat, with a food web to complete and one percentage calculation. Schemes are point-for-point and short: a mark per organism, a mark per arrow, a mark per resource. Stuck: draw the arrows you are sure of, because each one scores on its own.
